entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen9824" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Easter Festival Salutation and Discourse</title> <div sID="gen9825" type="x-p"/> Ps 80, which looks back into the time of the leading forth out of Egypt, is followed by another with the very same Asaphic thoroughly characteristic feature of a retrospective glance at Israel’s early history (cf. More particularly <reference osisRef="Ps.81.11">Psa 81:11</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.80.9">Psa 80:9</reference>). In Psalms 81 the lyric element of Ps 77 is combined with the didactic element of Ps 78. The unity of these Psalms is indubitable. All three have towards the close the appearance of being fragmentary. Fro the author delights to ascend to the height of his subject and to go down into the depth of it, without returning to the point from which he started. In Ps 77 Israel as a whole was called “the sons of Jacob and Joseph;” in Ps 78 we read “the sons of Ephraim” instead of the whole nation; here it is briefly called “Joseph.” This also indicates the one author. Then Psalms 81, exactly like <reference osisRef="Ps.79.1-Ps.79.13">Psa 79:1-13</reference>, is based upon the Pentateuchal history in Exodus and Deuteronomy. Jahve Himself speaks through the mouth of the poet, as He did once through the mouth of Moses - Asaph is κατ ̓ ἐξοχήν the prophet (חזה) among the psalmists. The transition from one form of speech to another which accompanies the rapid alternation of feelings, what the Arabs call <hi type="italic">talwı̂n el - chitab</hi>, “a colouring of a speech by a change of the persons,” is also characteristic of him, as later on of Micah (e.g., Mic 6:15.). <div eID="gen9825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9826" type="x-p"/> This Psalms 81 is according to ancient custom the Jewish New Year’s Psalm, the Psalm of the Feast of Trumpets (Num 29:1), therefore the Psalm of the first (and second) of Tishri; it is, however, a question whether the blowing of the horn (<hi type="italic">shophar</hi>) at the new moon, which it calls upon them to do, does not rather apply to the first of Nisan, to the ecclesiastical New Year. In the weekly liturgy of the Temple it was the Psalm for the Thursday. <div eID="gen9826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9827" type="x-p"/> The poet calls upon them to give a jubilant welcome to the approaching festive season, and in Psa 81:7. Jahve Himself makes Himself heard as the Preacher of the festival. He reminds those now living of His loving-kindness towards ancient Israel, and admonishes them not to incur the guilt of like unfaithfulness, in order that they may not lose the like tokens of His loving-kindness. What festive season is it? Either the Feast of the Passover or the Feast of Tabernacles; for it must be one of these two feasts which begin on the day of the full moon. Because it is one having reference to the redemption of Israel out of Egypt, the Targum, Talmud (more particularly <hi type="italic">Rosh ha - Shana</hi>, where this Psalm is much discussed), Midrash, and Sohar understand the Feast of Tabernacles; because <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.81.2-Ps.81.4">Psa 81:2-4</reference></hi> seem to refer to the new moon of the seventh month, which is celebrated before the other new moons (Num 10:10), as יום התּרוּעה (Num 29:1, cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.23.24">Lev 23:24</reference>), i.e., to the first of Tishri, the civil New Year; and the blowing of horns at the New Year, is, certainly not according to Scripture, but yet according to tradition (vid., Maimonides, <hi type="italic">Hilchoth Shophar</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.1.2">Psa 1:2</reference>), a very ancient arrangement. Nevertheless we must give up this reference of the Psalm to the first of Tishri and to the Feast of Tabernacles, which begins with the fifteenth of Tishri: - (1) Because between the high feast-day of the first of Tishri and the Feast of Tabernacles on the fifteenth to the twenty-first (twenty-second) of Tishri lies the great day of Atonement on the tenth of Tishri, which would be ignored, by greeting the festive season with a joyful noise from the first of Tishri forthwith to the fifteenth. (2) Because the remembrance of the redemption of Israel clings far more characteristically to the Feast of the Passover than to the Feast of Tabernacles. This latter appears in the oldest law-giving (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.16">Exo 23:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.22">Exo 34:22</reference>) as חג האסיף, i.e., as a feast of the ingathering of the autumn fruits, and therefore as the closing festival of the whole harvest; it does not receive the historical reference to the journey through the desert, and therewith its character of a feast of booths or arbours, until the addition in <reference osisRef="Lev.23.39-Lev.23.44">Lev 23:39-44</reference>, having reference to the carrying out of the celebration of the feasts in Canaan; whereas the feast which begins with the full moon of Nisan has, it is true, not been entirely free of all reference to agriculture, but from the very beginning bears the historical names פּסח and חג המּצּות.   (3) Because in the Psalm itself, viz., in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.81.6">Psa 81:6</reference></hi>, allusion is made to the fact which the Passover commemorates. <div eID="gen9827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9828" type="x-p"/> Concerning על־הגּתּית vid., on Psa 8:1. The symmetrical, stichic plan of the Psalm is clear: the schema is 11. 12. 12.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.81.1-Ps.81.5">Psa 81:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen9828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9829" type="x-p"/> The summons in <reference osisRef="Ps.81.2">Psa 81:2</reference> is addressed to the whole congregation, inasmuch as הריעוּ is not intended of the clanging of the trumpets, but as in Ezr 3:11, and frequently. The summons in <reference osisRef="Ps.81.3">Psa 81:3</reference> is addressed to the Levites, the appointed singers and musicians in connection with the divine services, <reference osisRef="2Chr.5.12">2Ch 5:12</reference>, and frequently. The summons in <reference osisRef="Ps.81.4">Psa 81:4</reference> is addressed to the priests, to whom was committed not only the blowing of the two (later on a hundred and twenty, vid., <reference osisRef="2Chr.5.12">2Ch 5:12</reference>) silver trumpets, but who appear also in <reference osisRef="Josh.6.4">Jos 6:4</reference> and elsewhere (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.47.6">Psa 47:6</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.28">2Ch 20:28</reference>) as the blowers of the shophar. The Talmud observes that since the destruction of the Temple the names of instruments שׁופרא and חצוצרתּא are wont to be confounded one for the other (<hi type="italic">B. Sabbath</hi> 36 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, <hi type="italic">Succa</hi> 34 <hi type="italic">a</hi>), and, itself confounding them, infers from Num 10:10 the duty and significance of the blowing of the shophar (<hi type="italic">B. Erachin</hi> 3 <hi type="italic">b</hi>). The lxx also renders both by σάλπιγξ; but the Biblical language mentions שׁופר and חצצרה, a horn (more especially a ram’s horn) and a (metal) trumpet, side by side in <reference osisRef="Ps.98.6">Psa 98:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.28">1Ch 15:28</reference>, and is therefore conscious of a difference between them. The Tôra says nothing of the employment of the shophar in connection with divine service, except that the commencement of every fiftieth year, which on this very account is called שׁנת היּבל, <hi type="italic">annus buccinae</hi>, is to be made known by the horn signal throughout all the land (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.9">Lev 25:9</reference>). But just as tradition by means of an inference from analogy derives the blowing of the shophar on the first of Tishri, the beginning of the common year, from this precept, so on the ground of the passage of the Psalm before us, assuming that בּחרשׁ, lxx ἐν νεομηνίᾳ, refers not to the first of Tishri but to the first of Nisan, we may suppose that the beginning of every month, but, in particular, the beginning of the month which was at the same time the beginning of the ecclesiastical year, was celebrated by a blowing of the shophar, as, according to Josephus, <hi type="italic">Bell</hi>. iv. 9, 12, the beginning and close of the Sabbath was announced from the top of the Temple by a priest with the salpinx. The poet means to say that the Feast of the Passover is to be saluted by the congregation with shouts of joy, by the Levites with music, and even beginning from the new moon (<hi type="italic">neomenia</hi>) of the Passover month with blowing of shophars, and that this is to be continued at the Feast of the Passover itself. The Feast of the Passover, for which Hupfeld devises a gloomy physiognomy,<note placement="foot">In the first of his <hi type="italic">Commentationes de primitiva et vera festorum apud Hebraeos ratione</hi>, 1851, 4to.</note> was a joyous festival, the Old Testament Christmas. <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.21">2Ch 30:21</reference> testifies to the exultation of the people and the boisterous music of the Levite priests, with which it was celebrated. According to Num 10:10, the trumpeting of the priests was connected with the sacrifices; and that the slaying of the paschal lambs took place amidst the <hi type="italic">Tantaratan</hi> of the priests (long-drawn notes interspersed with sharp shrill ones, תקיעה תרועה וקיעה), is expressly related of the post-exilic service at least.<note placement="foot">Vid., my essay on the Passover rites during the time of the second Temple in the <hi type="italic">Luther. Zeitschr</hi>. 1855; and cf. Armknecht, <hi type="italic">Die heilige Psalmidoe</hi> (1855), S. 5.</note> <div eID="gen9829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9830" type="x-p"/> The phrase נתן תּף proceeds from the phrase נתן קול, according to which נתן directly means: to attune, strike up, cause to be heard. Concerning כּסה (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.20">Pro 7:20</reference> כּסא) tradition is uncertain. The Talmudic interpretation (<hi type="italic">B. Rosh ha-Shana</hi> 8 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, <hi type="italic">Betza</hi> 16 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, and the Targum which is taken from it), according to which it is the day of the new moon (the first of the month), on which the moon hides itself, i.e., is not to be seen at all in the morning, and in the evening only for a short time immediately after sunset, and the interpretation that is adopted by a still more imposing array of authorities (lxx, Vulgate, Menahem, Rashi, Jacob Tam, Aben-Ezra, Parchon, and others), according to which a time fixed by computation (from כּסה = כּסס, <hi type="italic">computare</hi>) is so named in general, are outweighed by the usage of the Syriac, in which <hi type="italic">Keso</hi> denotes the full moon as the moon with covered, i.e., filled-up orb, and therefore the fifteenth of the month, but also the time from that point onwards, perhaps because then the moon covers itself, inasmuch as its shining surface appears each day less large (cf. the Peshîto, 1Ki 12:32 of the fifteenth day of the eighth month, <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.10">2Ch 7:10</reference> of the twenty-third day of the seventh month, in both instances of the Feast of Tabernacles), after which, too, in the passage before us it is rendered <hi type="italic">wa - b - kese</hi>, which a Syro-Arabic glossary (in Rosenmüller) explains <hi type="italic">festa quae sunt in medio mensis</hi>. The Peshîto here, like the Targum, proceeds from the reading חגּינוּ, which, following the lxx and the best texts, is to be rejected in comparison with the singular חגּנוּ. If, however, it is to be read chgnw, and כּסה (according to Kimchi with <hi type="italic">Segol</hi> not merely in the second syllable, but with double <hi type="italic">Segol</hi> כּסה, after the form טנא = טנא) signifies not <hi type="italic">interlunium</hi>, but <hi type="italic">plenilunium</hi> (instead of which also Jerome has <hi type="italic">in medio mense</hi>, and in <reference osisRef="Prov.7.20">Pro 7:20</reference>, <hi type="italic">in die plenae lunae</hi>, Aquila ἡμέρᾳ πανσελήνου), then what is meant is either the Feast of Tabernacles, which is called absolutely החג in 1Ki 8:2 (<reference osisRef="2Chr.5.3">2Ch 5:3</reference>) and elsewhere, or the Passover, which is also so called in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.29">Isa 30:29</reference> and elsewhere. Here, as <reference osisRef="Ps.81.5">Psa 81:5</reference> will convince us, the latter is intended, the Feast of unleavened bread, the porch of which, so to speak, is ערב פּסח together with the ליל שׁמּרים (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.42">Exo 12:42</reference>), the night from the fourteenth to the fifteenth of Nisan. In <reference osisRef="Ps.81.2">Psa 81:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.81.3">Psa 81:3</reference> they are called upon to give a welcome to this feast. The blowing of the shophar is to announce the commencement of the Passover month, and at the commencement of the Passover day which opens the Feast of unleavened bread it is to be renewed. The ל of ליום is not meant temporally, as perhaps in <reference osisRef="Job.21.30">Job 21:30</reference> : at the day = on the day; for why was it not ביום? It is rather: towards the day, but בכסה assumes that the day has already arrived; it is the same <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Ps.81.2">Psa 81:2</reference>, the blowing of the shophar is to concern this feast-day, it is to sound in honour of it.

It begins, as one would expect in a Passover speech, with a reference to the סבלות of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.1.11-Exod.1.14">Exo 1:11-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.5.4">Exo 5:4</reference>; Exo 6:6.), and to the duwd, the task-basket for the transport of the clay and of the bricks (<reference osisRef="Exod.1.14">Exo 1:14</reference>; Exo 5:7.).<note placement="foot">In the <hi type="italic">Papyrus Leydensis</hi> i. 346 the Israelites are called the “<hi type="italic">Aperiu</hi> (עברים), who dragged along the stones for the great watch-tower of the city of Rameses,” and in the <hi type="italic">Pap. Leyd.</hi> i. 349, according to Lauth, the “<hi type="italic">Aperiu</hi>, who dragged along the stones for the storehouse of the city of Rameses.”</note> <div eID="gen9832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9833" type="x-p"/> Out of such distress did He free the poor people who cried for deliverance (<reference osisRef="Exod.2.23-Exod.2.25">Exo 2:23-25</reference>); He answered them בּסתר רעם, i.e., not (according to <reference osisRef="Ps.22.22">Psa 22:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">Isa 32:2</reference>): affording them protection against the storm, but (according to <reference osisRef="Ps.18.12">Psa 18:12</reference>; Psa 77:17.): out of the thunder-clouds in which He at the same time revealed and veiled Himself, casting down the enemies of Israel with His lightnings, which is intended to refer pre-eminently to the passage through the Red Sea (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.77.19">Psa 77:19</reference>); and He proved them (אבחנך, with <hi type="italic">ŏ</hi> contracted from <hi type="italic">ō</hi>, cf. on <reference osisRef="Job.35.6">Job 35:6</reference>) at the waters of Merîbah, viz., whether they would trust Him further on after such glorious tokens of His power and loving-kindness. The name “<hi type="italic">Waters of Merı̂bah</hi>,” which properly is borne only by <hi type="italic">Merı̂bath Kadesh</hi>, the place of the giving of water in the fortieth year (Num 20:13; Num 27:14; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.51">Deu 32:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.8">Deu 33:8</reference>), is here transferred to the place of the giving of water in the first year, which was named <hi type="italic">Massah u - Merı̂bah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.7">Exo 17:7</reference>), as the remembrances of these two miracles, which took place under similar circumstances, in general blend together (vid., on Psa 95:8.). It is not now said that Israel did not act in response to the expectation of God, who had son wondrously verified Himself; the music, as Seal imports, here rises, and makes a long and forcible pause in what is being said. What now follows further, are, as the further progress of <reference osisRef="Ps.81.12">Psa 81:12</reference> shows, the words of God addressed to the Israel of the desert, which at the same time with its faithfulness are brought to the remembrance of the Israel of the present. העיד בּ, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.50.7">Psa 50:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.8.19">Deu 8:19</reference>, to bear testimony that concerns him against any one. אם (according to the sense, <hi type="italic">o si</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.95.7">Psa 95:7</reference>, which is in many ways akin to this Psalm) properly opens a searching question which wishes that the thing asked may come about (whether thou wilt indeed give me a willing hearing?!). In <reference osisRef="Ps.81.10">Psa 81:10</reference> the key-note of the revelation of the Law from Sinai is struck: the fundamental command which opens the decalogue demanded fidelity to Jahve and forbade idol-worship as the sin of sins. אל זר is an idol in opposition to the God of Israel as the true God; and אל נכר, a strange god in opposition to the true God as the God of Israel. To this one God Israel ought to yield itself all the more undividedly and heartily as it was more manifestly indebted entirely to Him, who in His condescension had chosen it, and in His wonder-working might had redeemed it (המּעלך, <hi type="italic">part.</hi> <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. with the <hi type="italic">eh</hi> elided, like הפּדך, <reference osisRef="Deut.13.6">Deu 13:6</reference>, and אכלך, from כּלּה, <reference osisRef="Exod.33.3">Exo 33:3</reference>); and how easy this submission ought to have been to it, since He desired nothing in return for the rich abundance of His good gifts, which satisfy and quicken body and soul, but only a wide-opened mouth, i.e., a believing longing, hungering for mercy and eager for salvation (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.131">Psa 119:131</reference>)!

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.81.11-Ps.81.16">Psa 81:11-16</reference> <div eID="gen9833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9834" type="x-p"/> The Passover discourse now takes a sorrowful and awful turn: Israel’s disobedience and self-will frustrated the gracious purpose of the commandments and promises of its God. “My people” and “Israel” alternate as in the complaint in Isa 1:3. לא־אבה followed by the dative, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.13.9">Deu 13:9</reference> ([8], ου ̓ συνθελήσεις αὐτῷ). Then God made their sin their punishment, by giving them over judicially (שׁלּח as in <reference osisRef="Job.8.4">Job 8:4</reference>) into the obduracy of their heart, which rudely shuts itself up against His mercy (from שׁרר, Aramaic שׁרר, Arabic <hi type="italic">sarra</hi>, to make firm = to cheer, make glad), so that they went on (cf. on the sequence of tense, <reference osisRef="Ps.61.8">Psa 61:8</reference>) in <hi type="italic">their</hi>, i.e., their own, egotistical, God-estranged determinations; the suffix is thus accented, as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Isa.65.2">Isa 65:2</reference>, cf. the borrowed passage <reference osisRef="Jer.7.24">Jer 7:24</reference>, and the same phrase in Mic 6:16. And now, because this state of unfaithfulness in comparison with God’s faithfulness has remained essentially the same even to to-day, the exalted Orator of the festival passes over forthwith to the generation of the present, and that, as is in accordance with the cheerful character of the feast, in a charmingly alluring manner. Whether we take לוּ in the signification of <hi type="italic">si</hi> (followed by the participle, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.12">2Sa 18:12</reference>), or like אם above in <reference osisRef="Ps.81.9">Psa 81:9</reference> as expressing a wish, <hi type="italic">o si</hi> (if but!), Psa 81:15. at any rate have the relation of the apodosis to it. From כּמעט (for a little, easily) it may be conjectured that the relation of Israel at that time to the nations did not correspond to the dignity of the nation of God which is called to subdue and rule the world in the strength of God. השׁיב signifies in this passage only to turn, not: to again lay upon. The meaning is, that He would turn the hand which is now chastening His people against those by whom He is chastening them (cf. on the usual meaning of the phrase, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.25">Isa 1:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.8">Amo 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.9">Jer 6:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.12">Eze 38:12</reference>). The promise in <reference osisRef="Ps.81.16">Psa 81:16</reference> relates to Israel and all the members of the nation. The haters of Jahve would be compelled reluctantly to submit themselves to Him, and their time would endure for ever. “Time” is equivalent to duration, and in this instance with the collateral notion of Prosperity, as elsewhere (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.22">Isa 13:22</reference>) of the term of punishment. One now expects that it should continue with ואאכילהוּ, in the tone of a promise. The Psalm, however, closes with an historical statement. For ויּאכילהו cannot signify<hi type="italic">et cibaret eum</hi>; it ought to be pronounced ויאכילהו. The pointing, like the lxx, Syriac, and Vulgate, takes v. 17 <hi type="italic">a</hi> (cf. Deu 32:13.) as a retrospect, and apparently rightly so. For even the Asaphic Ps 77 and 78 break off with historical pictures. V. 17 <hi type="italic">b</hi> is, accordingly, also to be taken as retrospective. The words of the poet in conclusion once more change into the words of God. The closing word runs אשׂבּיעך, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.50.8">Psa 50:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.31">Deu 4:31</reference>, and (with the exception of the <hi type="italic">futt. Hiph</hi>. of <hi type="italic">Lamed He</hi> verbs ending with <hi type="italic">ekka</hi>) usually. The Babylonian system of pointing nowhere recognises the suffix-form <hi type="italic">ekka</hi>. If the Israel of the present would hearken to the Lawgiver of Sinai, says v. 17, then would He renew to it the miraculous gifts of the time of the redemption under Moses. God’s Judgment upon the Gods of the Earth <div eID="gen9834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9835" type="x-p"/> As in Ps 81, so also in this Psalm (according to the Talmud the Tuesday Psalm of the Temple liturgy) God is introduced as speaking after the manner of the prophets. <reference osisRef="Ps.58.1-Ps.58.11">Psa 58:1-11</reference> and 94 are similar, but more especially <reference osisRef="Isa.3.13">Isa 3:13</reference>-15. Asaph the seer beholds how God, reproving, correcting, and threatening, appears against the chiefs of the congregation of His people, who have perverted the splendour of majesty which He has put upon them into tyranny. It is perfectly characteristic of Asaph (Ps 50; <reference osisRef="Ps.75.1-Ps.75.10">Psa 75:1-10</reference>; Ps 81) to plunge himself into the contemplation of the divine judgment, and to introduce God as speaking. There is nothing to militate against the Psalm being written by Asaph, David’s contemporary, except the determination not to allow to the לאסף of the inscription its most natural sense.
